## Purpose

A dependency-free, browser-based tic-tac-toe game played against the computer. It supports three single-board variants, not Ultimate Tic Tac Toe.

## Architecture and technologies

- **`TTT.html`** defines the interface and loads the stylesheet and script.
- **`TTT.css`** handles layout, board styling, the coin animation, focus indicators and reduced-motion styling.
- **`TTT.js`** manages game state, board rendering, win detection, turns and computer move selection. It uses plain JavaScript and the browser DOM.
- **`tests/game.test.js`** tests game logic and selected interactions using Node’s built-in test runner and a mocked DOM.
- **`README.md`** documents the rules and how to play and test.

There is no build step or runtime dependency. Open **`TTT.html`** in a browser to play. With Node.js installed, run **`node --test tests/game.test.js`** to run the tests.

## Existing functionality

- Choose a **3×3, 4×4 or 5×5** board. Changing size immediately starts a new game; **New game** retains the selected size.
- A coin toss determines who starts; the starting player is X.
- Winning requires three consecutive marks on 3×3 or 4×4, or four on 5×5, horizontally, vertically or diagonally. A full board without a winner is a draw.
- The computer uses full minimax on 3×3 and depth-limited search on larger boards, where perfect play is not guaranteed.
- The interface highlights a winning line, announces status updates, labels cells for assistive technology and supports reduced motion.
- Tokens prevent delayed actions from a previous game from changing a newly started game.

## Uncertainties and limitations

- The tests use a mocked DOM rather than a real browser; they do not establish visual layout, animation or assistive-technology behavior in practice.
- Larger-board AI responsiveness and playing strength can vary by device and position; there are no documented performance targets.
- Browser compatibility requirements and supported Node.js versions are not specified.
- The tests were reviewed but not run as part of this analysis.
on the 4x4 anf the 5x5 the marks should fall downwards to the lowest available row on the board

For **4×4 and 5×5**, a move would select a column, and the mark would land in its lowest empty cell—like Connect Four. The computer would follow the same rule, and full columns would be unavailable.

The **3×3 game** would stay as it is, and the existing win lengths would remain unchanged: three in a row on 4×4 and four on 5×5, including diagonals.

Should players be able to click **any cell in a column** to drop a mark there, or would you prefer separate controls above each column?
any cell

Got it. On **4×4 and 5×5**, clicking any cell in a column will drop your mark into that column’s lowest available row. Full columns won’t accept moves, and the computer will follow the same gravity rule.

The **3×3** game and existing win conditions remain unchanged.

Prepare a file change proposal from this discussion.

files.content:
# Tic-Tac-Toe

A browser-based game against the computer, using plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript. Open `TTT.html` in a browser to play; no build or dependencies are required.

Choose a 3×3, 4×4 or 5×5 board. The default is 3×3. Changing the size immediately discards the current game and starts a new one; **New game** keeps the selected size. A coin toss determines who starts, and X always plays first.

On 3×3, choose an empty cell. On 4×4 and 5×5, select any cell in a column, including an occupied cell: the mark lands in that column's lowest empty row. Full columns cannot be selected. The computer follows the same gravity rule.

Win with three consecutive marks on 3×3 or 4×4, or four consecutive marks on 5×5. Lines can appear anywhere horizontally, vertically or diagonally. A full board without a winner is a draw. The computer uses the same winning rules, with full minimax on 3×3 and a depth-limited search on 4×4 and 5×5, so its play on larger boards is not guaranteed to be perfect.

These are single-board variants, not Ultimate Tic Tac Toe.

## Tests

With Node.js installed, run `node --test tests/game.test.js tests/gravity.test.js`. The tests use only Node's built-in modules; the game itself does not require Node.js.

data.text: the fall to the bottom row should be animated!

A falling animation would make the gravity rule clearer. On **4×4 and 5×5**, each mark—including the computer’s—could visibly drop from the top of its column to the lowest available cell. The board would stay locked until it lands, then show any win or draw.

The **3×3 game** would remain unchanged, and players who prefer reduced motion would see the mark appear immediately.

Would you prefer a quick, smooth drop or a more playful bounce on landing?
playful bounce

A **playful bounce** it is. On 4×4 and 5×5, both players’ marks would drop from the top of the selected column and bounce as they land in the lowest available cell.

The board would stay locked during the animation, with wins and draws shown after landing. On 3×3, marks would appear as they do now; reduced-motion users would see gravity moves appear immediately.

## Purpose

A browser-based tic-tac-toe game against the computer, with 3×3, 4×4 and 5×5 single-board variants. It is not Ultimate Tic Tac Toe.

## Architecture and technologies

The game uses plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with no build step or runtime dependencies.

- **`TTT.html`** is the entry point and defines the controls, status and board container.
- **`TTT.css`** handles the responsive board, visual styling, coin-toss animation and focus indicators.
- **`TTT.js`** maintains game state, builds the board, applies moves and win rules, and chooses computer moves.
- **`README.md`** documents play and testing.
- **`tests/game.test.js`** and **`tests/gravity.test.js`** use Node’s built-in test runner and a mocked DOM. **`validation.json`** records the test command and criteria.

Open `TTT.html` in a browser to play. With Node.js installed, the documented test command is:

```sh
node --test tests/game.test.js tests/gravity.test.js
```

## Existing functionality

- A coin toss decides who starts; X always plays first. Changing board size starts a new game, while **New game** retains the selected size.
- On **3×3**, players select an empty cell directly. On **4×4 and 5×5**, selecting any cell in a non-full column places the mark in its lowest empty row; the computer follows the same rule.
- Three consecutive marks win on 3×3 and 4×4; four win on 5×5. Lines may be horizontal, vertical or diagonal. The game highlights a winning line and detects draws.
- The computer uses full minimax on 3×3 and depth-limited search on larger boards. Delayed actions from an earlier game are guarded against after a reset or size change.
- The interface includes labelled buttons, live status announcements, keyboard focus styling and reduced-motion handling for the coin toss.

## Uncertainties and limitations

- **The discussed falling-and-bouncing animation is not present in the current code.** Gravity moves currently appear immediately in their landing cells.
- Tests were reviewed but **not run** during this analysis. They use a mocked DOM, so they do not establish actual browser rendering, animation or assistive-technology behavior.
- Supported browser and Node.js versions, and performance targets for the larger-board AI, are not specified.
please propose the falling and bouncing animation

## Proposed animation

For **4×4 and 5×5**, both human and computer marks would:

1. Enter from the top of the selected column.
2. Fall to the lowest available cell, accelerating as they descend.
3. Bounce once or twice with diminishing height before settling.

The drop distance would reflect the landing row, so a mark landing near the top travels less far than one landing near the bottom. The board would remain locked until the mark settles; only then would the next turn, win or draw be announced.

**3×3** would stay unchanged. With **reduced motion** enabled, marks would appear immediately in their landing cells. Starting a new game or changing board size during a drop would cancel the old animation and prevent it from affecting the new game.

A quick, playful drop of roughly **400–600 ms**, including the bounce, should feel responsive without slowing play.


## Existing functionality

- A coin toss decides who starts; X always plays first. Changing board size starts a new game, while **New game** retains the selected size.
- On **3×3**, players select an empty cell directly. On **4×4 and 5×5**, selecting any cell in a non-full column places the mark in its lowest empty row; the computer follows the same rule.

# Tic-Tac-Toe

A browser-based game against the computer, using plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript. Open `TTT.html` in a browser to play; no build or dependencies are required.

Choose a 3×3, 4×4 or 5×5 board. The default is 3×3. Changing the size immediately discards the current game and starts a new one; **New game** keeps the selected size. A coin toss determines who starts, and X always plays first.

On 3×3, choose an empty cell. On 4×4 and 5×5, select any cell in a column, including an occupied cell: the mark lands in that column's lowest empty row. Full columns cannot be selected. The computer follows the same gravity rule. Both players' marks fall and bounce into place; the board stays locked until the mark settles. With reduced motion enabled, marks appear immediately. Resetting or changing size cancels a drop.

Win with three consecutive marks on 3×3 or 4×4, or four consecutive marks on 5×5. Lines can appear anywhere horizontally, vertically or diagonally. A full board without a winner is a draw. The computer uses the same winning rules, with full minimax on 3×3 and a depth-limited search on 4×4 and 5×5, so its play on larger boards is not guaranteed to be perfect.

These are single-board variants, not Ultimate Tic Tac Toe.

## Tests

With Node.js installed, run `node --test tests/game.test.js tests/gravity.test.js tests/animation.test.js`. The tests use only Node's built-in modules; the game itself does not require Node.js. They mock the DOM; visual animation and assistive-technology behavior should also be checked in a browser.
